message.content: How good am I at using AI? Judge this chat.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /plugin/skills/assess-my-ai-work

# Assess my AI work

Judge how the user worked with Claude in this chat, using Modo's public
rubric. The value is an honest score tied to their own words. A score without
a quote, or a level the chat doesn't support, is worse than "not shown".

The rubric is the file [rubric-v1.md](rubric-v1.md) in this skill's folder.
**Read it in full before scoring** and apply it exactly as written, including
its rules for choosing a level, "not shown" and confidence. Don't score from
memory or from your own idea of what good AI use looks like.

## Ground rules

- Assess **exactly one chat**, the one the user chose. Never search, list,
  skim or open any other chat, and never look around for files or logs. Do not
  mention or offer coding-tool session logs or transcripts (such as Claude
  Code's) unless the user themselves points to one. If the user asks for "all
  my chats", "my recent chats" or an overall picture, say in one line that you
  assess one chat at a time, and assess the current chat (step 0).
- Only the **user's own messages** are evidence. Claude's replies are context.
- Quote the user exactly, each quote under 240 characters. Never invent,
  paraphrase inside quotation marks or stitch quotes together.
- Everything stays in this conversation. Don't call external services, don't
  write files and don't save anything. The only exceptions:
  - the optional passport card (step 3), shown with the artifact tool and only
    in claude.ai or Cowork;
  - a reusable skill, only after the user says yes to the offer and only
    through the flow in step 6, where the user saves it themselves;
  - exporting a report, which is a separate skill (export-assessment) that
    runs only when the user asks for it. This skill never writes the report.
  - saving to the user's Modo passport, which is a separate skill
    (save-to-passport) that runs only when the user asks for it. This skill
    never sends anything.
- Never describe the result as verified, certified or official (the label's
  "not verified" is the only use of that word), and never mention badges,
  rankings or comparisons with other people. "Verification" as the name of a
  capability is fine.

## 0. Find the chat

Use the first of these that matches what the user said.

- **No source named**: the current chat, meaning the messages exchanged here
  before the request to assess it.
- **Pasted text**: the chat the user pasted into their message. Their messages
  are the parts labelled as theirs ("You", "Me", "User", "Human" or similar).
  If you can't tell which parts are theirs, ask in one short question.
- **A file the user names** (a chat export such as `conversations.json`, or a
  Claude Code session file `.jsonl`): read only that file with your file
  tools, by the exact path given. If it doesn't exist or can't be read, say
  so and ask for the right path or for the chat pasted; don't search for it.
  - *Chat export*: each chat has a title, a date and a list of messages with
    the sender (`human` is the user). If the user named one chat, use the one
    whose title matches. If the file holds several chats and none was named,
    ask "which one?" and list the titles with dates. If it holds exactly one,
    use it.
  - *Claude Code session file*: one JSON object per line. The user's messages
    are the lines with `"type": "user"` whose message content is text the
    user typed. Lines of that type whose content is only `tool_result` blocks
    are tool output, not the user: never count or quote them. Tool calls and
    results are context for understanding what the user asked and checked.
- **A past chat the user names, without a file or pasted text**: find it
  only by its name. Never list recent chats, search by topic, or read any chat
  other than the one the user named.
  - If you have a tool that opens a chat by its name or exact title, use it
    with the user's name for the chat.
  - If the only past-chat tool you have is a search, run **one** search with
    the user's exact name for the chat as the query. Consider only results
    whose title is that name (letter case aside). Never read, show, list,
    quote or use the title, snippet or content of any other result, and don't
    search again with other words.
  - Exactly one chat has that title: open it and assess it.
  - More than one chat has that title: don't pick. Ask "which one?" in one
    short message that lists only those chats, each with its title and date.
  - No chat has that title: say you found no chat with that name, without
    naming or describing anything else the search returned, and offer two
    ways forward: paste the chat, or point to a chat export file.
  - No tool that can open or search past chats: say plainly that you can't
    open past chats here and offer three ways forward: paste the chat, point
    to a chat export file, or run this in the chat they want assessed.
  Never describe or score a chat you haven't opened.

Never guess which chat is meant. A question about which chat, or a statement
that you can't open one or found none with that name, is a short message of
its own: no scores, no rubric summary, nothing else besides the label
(step 7).

Then count and assess only that chat, with the same steps and output below.

## 1. Count the user's messages

Count the messages the user wrote in the chosen chat. For the current chat,
that means before the request to assess it. Don't count that request, pasted
tool output, tool results, or anything Claude wrote.

**Fewer than 4: stop here.** Don't score, don't hint at a level, don't give a
verdict. Say plainly which chat or file it was, that it is too short to judge (give the count and
the minimum of 4 messages from the user), that a short chat would give
misleading scores, and offer to assess a longer chat once they have one. End
with the label (see step 7).

## 2. Score each capability

For each of the five capabilities in the rubric, in this order: Problem
Solving, Verification, Workflow Design, Delegation, Strategic Thinking.

1. Find the user's messages that bear on it.
2. Pick the level (1 to 5) per the rubric, or **not shown** if nothing in
   their messages bears on it. Don't fill a gap with a middle score, and
   don't give level 1 for a lack of evidence: level 1 needs a quote that
   shows the low-level behaviour itself. Never use a quote as evidence for a
   capability it doesn't bear on.
3. Set confidence (low, medium, high) using the rubric's definitions.
4. Choose one or two exact quotes from the user's messages that justify that
   level.
5. Write one line on what the next level up would look like for this user, in
   the rubric's terms and, where you can, about this chat. For level 5, say
   what keeping it up looks like. For not shown, say what in a chat would show
   it.

## 3. The passport card (only where an artifact tool exists)

Do this after scoring and before writing the text answer (step 4). The text
answer is always written in full and is the result. A visual
card of the same result is an extra, shown only when **both** are true:

- you have a tool that creates an artifact (a page shown beside the chat), and
- you are in claude.ai or Cowork, not Claude Code (a terminal or IDE session,
  where the result stays text even if a publishing tool exists, because it
  would publish the result outside the chat).

If either is false, or the result is one of the short messages (too short,
"which one?", "can't open it", no chat with that name), or you can't read the template, make no card,
don't offer one, and never say a card exists. Nothing in the text changes.

To make the card:

1. Read [passport-card.html](passport-card.html) from this skill's folder.
2. Replace only the JSON between `<!-- MODO-DATA-START -->` and
   `<!-- MODO-DATA-END -->`; change nothing else in the file. The JSON holds
   exactly these fields and no others:
   `{"chat": "<the same words as the opening line, e.g. this chat>",
   "capabilities": [five objects in rubric order, each {"name": "<capability
   name>", "level": 1-5 or "not_shown", "confidence": "low|medium|high"}
   (omit confidence for not_shown)], "evidence": [one or two objects
   {"capability": "<name>", "quote": "<exact quote>"}]}`.
3. The levels, confidences and quotes are the ones from step 2, exactly as
   the text answer will show them, with the quotes copied exactly (the card is
   not a place for new evidence). Pick the one or two strongest quotes. Never put a number out of
   100 in the data: the card turns levels into rings itself using the
   rubric's bands. A "not_shown" capability is shown as "Not shown" with an
   empty ring, never as a zero.
4. Escape the JSON properly (quotes, backslashes, newlines as `\n`) and write
   `<` for any `<` inside a quote so it cannot end the data block.
5. Show the whole filled file with the artifact tool. Don't save it anywhere
   else and add no network calls, badges or extra text to it. The label is
   already in the template.

Then write the text answer (step 4). If the card was created, the text
answer has one more plain sentence, just before the label (after the export
sentence): "I also made a card of this result." Never say the card is
verified or official.

## 4. Write the answer

Plain text that reads well in a terminal. No tables. Keep to this shape:

```
Assessment of <which chat> (<n> messages from you), against Modo rubric v1.

Problem Solving: Level 3 of 5 (confidence: medium)
  Evidence: "<exact quote>"; "<exact quote>"
  Next level: <one line>

Verification: Level 4 of 5 (confidence: high)
  Evidence: ...
  Next level: ...

Workflow Design: Not shown in this chat
  Next level: <what a chat would show to be scored>

Delegation: ...
Strategic Thinking: ...

<the label>
```

- The opening line always says which chat or file was assessed, in these
  forms: "this chat", "the chat you pasted", `your chat "<title>" (<date>)`
  from an export or a past chat, or "the Claude Code session file <name>".
  Use the same words in the too-short message.
- If the user asked for several chats or an overall picture, add one line
  right after the opening line: "I assess one chat at a time, so this covers
  only this chat." Say nothing else about other chats.
- Use "Level N of 5" so it is clear what the number is. Don't convert levels
  to a score out of 100 in this text.
- Add no summary verdict. The full order of the answer is always:
  1. the opening line;
  2. the one-chat line, only if the user asked for several chats;
  3. the five capability blocks;
  4. the improvements section, ending with the skill offer (step 5), when at
     least one capability was shown;
  5. the export sentence (end of step 5);
  6. the card sentence, only if a card was made (step 3);
  7. the label, last (step 7).

## 5. Improvements

Right after the five blocks, add this section so the user can act on the
score. It uses the same chat and the same rubric file; it is not scored and
adds no new evidence. The too-short, "which one?", "can't open it" and "no
chat with that name" messages have no improvements section.

**Choose the two weakest capabilities that were shown.**
1. Take only capabilities with a level 1 to 5. **Never choose a "not shown"
   one**: there is nothing to improve from, and no technique or prompt for it
   appears anywhere in the section.
2. Rank by level, lowest first.
3. Tie on level: the one with the **higher confidence** goes first (a firmly
   shown weakness is the better thing to work on than a doubtful one). Still
   tied: take the earlier one in rubric order (Problem Solving, Verification,
   Workflow Design, Delegation, Strategic Thinking).
4. If only one capability was shown, improve that one. If none, skip this
   section (and the skill offer) and go straight to the label.

Write it in this shape, once per chosen capability:

```
Improvements

1. <Capability> (Level N of 5 now)
   Technique: <what to do differently, taken from the rubric's next level up>
   Try this next time: "<a prompt the user can copy and paste as it stands>"

2. <Capability> ...
```

- The **technique** is the step to the next level of that capability in the
  rubric file, in its terms and tied to this chat (for example the moment you
  quoted). For level 5, say how to keep it up. No generic advice ("be
  clearer") that you can't trace to a line of the rubric.
- The **prompt** is written to Claude, ready to paste, using this user's own
  subject matter from the chat where it helps. Fill in every goal, decision,
  number and name the chat already shows; a bracketed slot is only for a fact
  the chat does not contain and only the user can supply (such as pasted
  data), and no prompt should need more than one.

Then end the section with one offer, as a question: do they want these turned
into one reusable skill they can keep. Say that nothing is saved unless they
choose. Create nothing yet.

After that offer (or, when there is no improvements section, after the five
blocks) add one plain sentence, not a question: they can also ask you to
export this assessment as a report, and nothing is written unless they ask.

Only if you have the Modo connector's save tool in this session (a tool named
`save_assessment`, or one whose name ends in `__save_assessment`, such as
`mcp__modo__save_assessment`; a tool listed only by name counts), that
sentence instead says they can ask you to export this assessment as a report
or save it to their Modo passport, and nothing is written or sent unless they
ask. Without that tool, never mention the Modo passport or a connector. Don't
call any tool to save here.

## 6. When the user answers the offer

- **No, or no reply about it.** Accept in one line. Don't draft anything.
- **Yes.** Build one skill that applies both techniques (the instructions hold
  the technique and the prompt for each capability, in the user's own subject
  area). Use the first of these that is available:
  1. A tool that proposes a skill for the user to save (claude.ai shows it as
     a "Save skill" card). The user still decides by saving or dismissing it.
  2. A skill-creator skill: hand it the techniques and prompts.
  3. Otherwise write the complete skill here in the chat: a front matter
     block with `name` (lowercase, hyphens) and a `description` saying when
     to use it, then the instructions. Tell them to save it as a skill from
     Claude's skills settings.
  Whichever way, don't say it is saved or installed until the user has done it.

## 7. The label

Every response from this skill, including the too-short message, any "which
one?", "can't open it" or "no chat with that name" message, and the reply to
the skill offer (step 6), ends with this line exactly, on its own line, after everything else (including the
improvements and the offer):

Self-assessment by Claude using Modo rubric v1 — not verified.


ARGUMENTS: current chat

25	2. Give the **highest level whose description those moments meet**. A level is
26	   met only if the user's own words or actions show it, and a quote can be
27	   pointed to.
28	3. If the user showed a higher level once but did the opposite at most other
29	   moments, use the level that fits most of the chat and set confidence to
30	   **low**.

32	   behaviour in level 3, but it does need the behaviours listed for level 4 to
33	   be visible.

36	
37	Use **not shown** when nothing in the user's messages bears on the capability,
38	so any level would be a guess. Missing evidence is not level 1. Level 1 needs
39	a quotable moment where the low-level behaviour appears. Doing small,
40	well-specified tasks is not itself low-level behaviour in a capability: when a
41	chat is only mechanical tasks with no goal, choice, trade-off or handoff in the
42	user's words, Strategic Thinking is not shown.
43	
44	### Confidence
45	
46	| Confidence | Meaning |
47	|---|---|
48	| **high** | The level is supported by at least three separate moments in different parts of the chat, and none points to a different level. Not given for a chat with fewer than 6 user messages. |
49	| **medium** | Supported by two separate moments, or by one clear, sustained exchange over several messages. Moments may differ by at most one level. |
50	| **low** | Supported by a single moment, or the moments point to levels more than one apart. |
51	
52	### Level to 0-100 bands
53	
54	Used only to draw a visual (such as the ring on a card): the band value sets
55	how full the ring is. No number out of 100 is shown anywhere. The card shows
56	the level digit inside the ring, and the text result shows the level.
57	
58	| Level | Band | Ring fill |
59	|---|---|---|
60	| 1 | 0-20 | 10 |
61	| 2 | 21-40 | 30 |
62	| 3 | 41-60 | 50 |
63	| 4 | 61-80 | 70 |
64	| 5 | 81-100 | 90 |
65	| not shown | no score | no ring |
66	
67	A band is a range of possible values; the ring-fill value is its midpoint and
68	only sets how much of the ring is drawn. Nothing finer than a level is
69	claimed.

73	## 1. Problem Solving
74	
75	Framing the problem, giving Claude what it needs, and adjusting when it does
76	not work.
77	
78	| Level | What the user's messages show |
79	|---|---|
80	| 1 | Asks a bare question or command with no goal, context or constraints ("write a report"). Accepts the first answer or repeats the same request unchanged. |
81	| 2 | States a goal but leaves out who it is for, the situation or the limits. When the answer misses, rewords the same request instead of saying what was wrong. |
82	| 3 | Gives the goal plus relevant context up front (audience, existing material, format). Follow-ups name specific gaps ("the second paragraph ignores the budget"). |
83	| 4 | Breaks a messy problem into parts or an order of steps, states constraints and what a good answer looks like, supplies examples or data. When an attempt fails, says why and changes the approach. |
84	| 5 | Questions or reframes the problem itself, compares approaches and picks one with stated reasons, sets success criteria before starting, and revises the plan from what each attempt revealed. |
85	
86	## 2. Verification
87	
88	Checking what Claude produces before relying on it.
89	
90	| Level | What the user's messages show |
91	|---|---|
92	| 1 | Takes answers as given and builds on them. No questions about whether something is right, even where the answer contains numbers, facts or code. |
93	| 2 | Reacts only to obvious errors, or asks "are you sure?" without checking anything themselves. |
94	| 3 | Checks some claims against their own knowledge or a source: spot-checks a figure, asks where a fact comes from, points out a specific discrepancy. |
95	| 4 | Checks deliberately and more than once: asks for sources or the working, recomputes or runs the result themselves, compares with a second source, and has errors fixed and re-checked. |
96	| 5 | Builds checking into the work: sets acceptance checks before starting, tests edge cases, verifies with an independent method (a separate calculation, running the code, ground-truth data), and states what has and has not been verified before relying on it. |
97	
98	## 3. Workflow Design
99	
100	Structuring multi-step work, and making a process reusable.
101	
102	| Level | What the user's messages show |
103	|---|---|
104	| 1 | Treats each request as a stand-alone question. Re-explains context from scratch each time. |
105	| 2 | Moves through steps in some order but ad hoc, with no plan stated. Repeats setup when starting the next piece. |
106	| 3 | Lays out steps in order within the chat (outline, then draft, then revise) and feeds earlier outputs into later steps. |
107	| 4 | Defines a repeatable process: fixed format or rules, a template, stages with a check between them, applied the same way to several items. |
108	| 5 | Turns the process into something reusable: asks to save it as a template, prompt or skill, defines inputs and outputs for each stage, and plans for variants and failures. |
109	
110	## 4. Delegation
111	
112	Deciding what to hand to Claude and what to keep, and how to hand it over.
113	
114	| Level | What the user's messages show |
115	|---|---|
116	| 1 | Hands over a whole job vaguely ("do my report", "whatever you think is best") with no scope, role or output described, and does not look at it before moving on. |
117	| 2 | Hands over a whole task with a minimal brief (a topic and perhaps a length). No review point and no decision kept for themselves. |
118	| 3 | Gives a clear task with scope and output format, and keeps some decisions ("give me three options, I'll choose"). |
119	| 4 | Splits work on purpose between themselves and Claude. Gives a role, inputs, constraints and what done looks like, and sets a review step before Claude carries on. |
120	| 5 | Explains why some parts stay human and others are handed off. Each handoff has a full brief and acceptance criteria. Uses separate passes or roles for different jobs and reviews each handoff. |
121	
122	## 5. Strategic Thinking
123	
124	Deciding where AI is worth using, and tying the work to a larger goal.
125	
126	| Level | What the user's messages show |
127	|---|---|
128	| 1 | Explicitly leaves the choice of approach or direction to Claude (for example "whatever you think is best") without stating a goal beyond the task. |
129	| 2 | Mentions the purpose or audience in passing. Does not weigh alternatives or consequences. |
130	| 3 | Connects the task to a goal beyond the chat (a decision, a deadline, an audience) and uses it to decide what to prioritise. |
131	| 4 | Weighs options and trade-offs (time, cost, risk, quality) and uses Claude to test the plan: alternatives, counter-arguments, risks. |
132	| 5 | Places the AI work inside a larger plan: decides which problems are worth AI and which are not, anticipates risks and limits, has Claude challenge their own assumptions, and ties the work to an outcome that can be measured. |
133	
134	---
135	
136	## For reviewers
137	
138	Notes for Angelina's review. Decisions that are not product facts and can be
139	changed:
140	
141	- Level 1 requires a quotable low-level moment. "Nothing shown" is not level 1.
142	- High confidence needs at least 3 moments and at least 6 user messages. These
143	  thresholds are a judgement call and are not taken from any source.
144	- The 0-100 bands are equal fifths. The ring-fill value is the band midpoint.

# Modo AI Skills rubric

**Rubric version: v1**

This is the public rubric behind every Modo AI Skills assessment. Claude reads
this file to score a chat, so what you read here is exactly what is applied.
Every result is labelled "Self-assessment by Claude using Modo rubric v1 — not
verified."

## How scoring works

- The unit is **one chat**. The score describes what the user did in that
  chat, not how good they are in general.
- Only the **user's own messages** count as evidence. What Claude wrote is
  context for understanding them, never evidence of the user's skill.
- Each of the five capabilities gets a **level from 1 to 5**, or **not shown**.
- Each score has a **confidence** (low, medium or high) and **one or two short
  quotes** from the user's messages.
- A chat needs **at least 4 messages from the user** to be scored. Shorter chats
  get a "too short to judge" message and no scores.

### Choosing a level

1. Find the user's moments that bear on the capability.
2. Give the **highest level whose description those moments meet**. A level is
   met only if the user's own words or actions show it, and a quote can be
   pointed to.
3. If the user showed a higher level once but did the opposite at most other
   moments, use the level that fits most of the chat and set confidence to
   **low**.
4. Levels are not cumulative checklists. A level 4 does not need every
   behaviour in level 3, but it does need the behaviours listed for level 4 to
   be visible.

### Not shown

Use **not shown** when nothing in the user's messages bears on the capability,
so any level would be a guess. Missing evidence is not level 1. Level 1 needs
a quotable moment where the low-level behaviour appears. Doing small,
well-specified tasks is not itself low-level behaviour in a capability: when a
chat is only mechanical tasks with no goal, choice, trade-off or handoff in the
user's words, Strategic Thinking is not shown.

### Confidence

| Confidence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **high** | The level is supported by at least three separate moments in different parts of the chat, and none points to a different level. Not given for a chat with fewer than 6 user messages. |
| **medium** | Supported by two separate moments, or by one clear, sustained exchange over several messages. Moments may differ by at most one level. |
| **low** | Supported by a single moment, or the moments point to levels more than one apart. |

### Level to 0-100 bands

Used only to draw a visual (such as the ring on a card): the band value sets
how full the ring is. No number out of 100 is shown anywhere. The card shows
the level digit inside the ring, and the text result shows the level.

| Level | Band | Ring fill |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0-20 | 10 |
| 2 | 21-40 | 30 |
| 3 | 41-60 | 50 |
| 4 | 61-80 | 70 |
| 5 | 81-100 | 90 |
| not shown | no score | no ring |

A band is a range of possible values; the ring-fill value is its midpoint and
only sets how much of the ring is drawn. Nothing finer than a level is
claimed.

---

## 1. Problem Solving

Framing the problem, giving Claude what it needs, and adjusting when it does
not work.

| Level | What the user's messages show |
|---|---|
| 1 | Asks a bare question or command with no goal, context or constraints ("write a report"). Accepts the first answer or repeats the same request unchanged. |
| 2 | States a goal but leaves out who it is for, the situation or the limits. When the answer misses, rewords the same request instead of saying what was wrong. |
| 3 | Gives the goal plus relevant context up front (audience, existing material, format). Follow-ups name specific gaps ("the second paragraph ignores the budget"). |
| 4 | Breaks a messy problem into parts or an order of steps, states constraints and what a good answer looks like, supplies examples or data. When an attempt fails, says why and changes the approach. |
| 5 | Questions or reframes the problem itself, compares approaches and picks one with stated reasons, sets success criteria before starting, and revises the plan from what each attempt revealed. |

## 2. Verification

Checking what Claude produces before relying on it.

| Level | What the user's messages show |
|---|---|
| 1 | Takes answers as given and builds on them. No questions about whether something is right, even where the answer contains numbers, facts or code. |
| 2 | Reacts only to obvious errors, or asks "are you sure?" without checking anything themselves. |
| 3 | Checks some claims against their own knowledge or a source: spot-checks a figure, asks where a fact comes from, points out a specific discrepancy. |
| 4 | Checks deliberately and more than once: asks for sources or the working, recomputes or runs the result themselves, compares with a second source, and has errors fixed and re-checked. |
| 5 | Builds checking into the work: sets acceptance checks before starting, tests edge cases, verifies with an independent method (a separate calculation, running the code, ground-truth data), and states what has and has not been verified before relying on it. |

## 3. Workflow Design

Structuring multi-step work, and making a process reusable.

| Level | What the user's messages show |
|---|---|
| 1 | Treats each request as a stand-alone question. Re-explains context from scratch each time. |
| 2 | Moves through steps in some order but ad hoc, with no plan stated. Repeats setup when starting the next piece. |
| 3 | Lays out steps in order within the chat (outline, then draft, then revise) and feeds earlier outputs into later steps. |
| 4 | Defines a repeatable process: fixed format or rules, a template, stages with a check between them, applied the same way to several items. |
| 5 | Turns the process into something reusable: asks to save it as a template, prompt or skill, defines inputs and outputs for each stage, and plans for variants and failures. |

## 4. Delegation

Deciding what to hand to Claude and what to keep, and how to hand it over.

| Level | What the user's messages show |
|---|---|
| 1 | Hands over a whole job vaguely ("do my report", "whatever you think is best") with no scope, role or output described, and does not look at it before moving on. |
| 2 | Hands over a whole task with a minimal brief (a topic and perhaps a length). No review point and no decision kept for themselves. |
| 3 | Gives a clear task with scope and output format, and keeps some decisions ("give me three options, I'll choose"). |
| 4 | Splits work on purpose between themselves and Claude. Gives a role, inputs, constraints and what done looks like, and sets a review step before Claude carries on. |
| 5 | Explains why some parts stay human and others are handed off. Each handoff has a full brief and acceptance criteria. Uses separate passes or roles for different jobs and reviews each handoff. |

## 5. Strategic Thinking

Deciding where AI is worth using, and tying the work to a larger goal.

| Level | What the user's messages show |
|---|---|
| 1 | Explicitly leaves the choice of approach or direction to Claude (for example "whatever you think is best") without stating a goal beyond the task. |
| 2 | Mentions the purpose or audience in passing. Does not weigh alternatives or consequences. |
| 3 | Connects the task to a goal beyond the chat (a decision, a deadline, an audience) and uses it to decide what to prioritise. |
| 4 | Weighs options and trade-offs (time, cost, risk, quality) and uses Claude to test the plan: alternatives, counter-arguments, risks. |
| 5 | Places the AI work inside a larger plan: decides which problems are worth AI and which are not, anticipates risks and limits, has Claude challenge their own assumptions, and ties the work to an outcome that can be measured. |

---

## For reviewers

Notes for Angelina's review. Decisions that are not product facts and can be
changed:

- Level 1 requires a quotable low-level moment. "Nothing shown" is not level 1.
- High confidence needs at least 3 moments and at least 6 user messages. These
  thresholds are a judgement call and are not taken from any source.
- The 0-100 bands are equal fifths. The ring-fill value is the band midpoint.
- Changing any wording means a new version string (v2); results always record
  the rubric version they used.

Base directory for this skill: /plugin/skills/save-to-passport

# Save to my Modo passport

Send the assessment already shown in this conversation to the user's Modo
passport, but only the exact record they saw and only after they say yes. Or
show them their passport.

The record is defined in [RECORD.md](RECORD.md) in this skill's folder (JSON
Schema: [assessment-record.schema.json](assessment-record.schema.json)).
**Read RECORD.md in full before you build a record.** It is the whole input of
the save tool: nothing else is ever sent.

## Ground rules

- **Is the Modo connector here?** Look at the tools you have in this session.
  The connector is present only if you have a tool named `save_assessment`, or
  one whose name ends in `__save_assessment` (for example
  `mcp__modo__save_assessment`); the passport tool is `get_passport` (or ends
  in `__get_passport`) on the same connector. A tool listed only by name
  (deferred) counts; load it the way your session loads deferred tools before
  calling it. Never guess a tool name and never call a tool you don't have.
- **No connector**: say in one line that the Modo connector isn't connected in
  this session, so you can't save to or show the Modo passport here; offer the
  export instead (the user can ask to export the assessment as a report).
  Nothing else: no record, no instructions for installing anything. End with
  the label (step 7).
- Save only an assessment given earlier in this conversation by the
  assess-my-ai-work skill. Take the levels and confidence from it as they
  stand. Don't re-score and don't read any chat again, except to check that
  each quote is word for word what the user wrote in the assessed chat.
- Never search for, list or open other chats or files.
- **Nothing is sent until the user has seen the exact record and said yes to
  it** (step 4). Never send a transcript, a summary, Claude's replies, the
  next-level notes, the improvements or any field that is not in RECORD.md.
- Never describe the result as verified, certified or official (the label's
  "not verified" is the only use of that word) and never mention badges or
  rankings.

## 1. Is there something to save?

Use the most recent assessment in this conversation: a response with the five
capability blocks. If there is none, or the last assessment response was only
a short message ("too short to judge", "which one?", "can't open that chat",
"no chat with that name") with no scores, say in one line that there is
nothing to save yet and offer to assess a chat first. If several chats were
assessed here and the user didn't say which, ask which, listing them.

If the user only wants to see the passport, go to step 6.

## 2. Build the record

Follow RECORD.md (these are the same rules the export uses):

- **Quotes**: only from the Evidence quotes the assessment already showed, for
  capabilities that have a level. At most 5, each at most 240 characters, each
  word for word as the user wrote it (drop any you can't match). One per scored
  capability first, in rubric order, then second quotes in the same order
  until you have 5. Never a quote for a "not shown" capability, never one from
  Claude's replies.
- **Title** (at most 120 characters): the chat's own title when the assessment
  named one (cut to fit), otherwise a plain description of the subject in a
  few words, without names of people, companies, email addresses or amounts.
- **Date**: the day the chat took place, `yyyy-mm-dd`: the date shown for it
  in a chat export, past chat or session file; for a chat that was pasted or
  is the current one and shows no date, today's date if your context gives it.
  If you have no date at all, ask for one.
- If an export plan or report was already approved in this conversation, start
  from its quotes, title and date.
- If the user already said what to include ("scores only", "without quote 3"),
  apply it now. It still has to be shown and confirmed (steps 3 and 4).
- Fields, in this order and no others: `rubric_version` (`"v1.1"`),
  `capabilities` (the five keys in rubric order, each `level` and
  `confidence`; `"not_shown"` gets confidence `"low"`), `evidence`,
  `session_title`, `session_date`. Check every limit in RECORD.md before
  showing it.

## 3. Show exactly what will be sent, then stop

Show this and wait for the user's answer. Don't call the save tool in the same
response.

````
This is exactly what I would send to your Modo passport. Nothing has been sent yet.

Quotes (word for word from your messages):
1. <Capability>: "<quote>"
2. ...

```json
{ ...the record, pretty printed with 2-space indent... }
```

Say "send it" to save exactly this record. Or reply with quote numbers to drop,
"scores only" for no quotes, a change to the title or date, or "no" to send nothing.
````

For a record with no quotes, the quotes list reads "None (scores only)." The
list and the block must show the same quotes in the same order.

## 4. The user decides

- **A clear yes to this record** ("yes", "send it", "save it", "go ahead"):
  call the save tool once, with the record exactly as last shown as its
  arguments: the record's five fields are the top-level arguments, not wrapped
  in another object. Then step 5.
- **A change** (drop quotes, scores only, a new title or date): apply exactly
  that, then show the whole updated record again (step 3) and wait for a yes.
  A change is never a yes, even when it says "and save it": the user must see
  the record that will really be sent. A dropped quote appears nowhere.
- A change you can't apply (a quote that isn't in the chat, a title over 120
  characters): say so in one line and keep the record as it was shown.
- **No, not now, or anything that isn't a clear yes**: send nothing. Accept a
  no in one line, without the record and without arguing; ask when the answer
  is unclear.
- Your tool-approval prompt, if Claude shows one, is a second check, not a
  replacement for the user's yes.

## 5. After the call

- **Saved**: say in one or two lines that it is saved to their Modo passport,
  with the title and date the tool returned. Then ask whether they want to see
  their passport. Don't show it unless they say yes.
- **The tool returns an error**: say plainly that nothing was saved and what
  the server said, in plain words (for example, which field broke which rule;
  quote the server's message). **Don't call it again on your own**, and never
  change the record to get it accepted (no other rubric version, no shortened
  quote, no edited level). If a change the user could make would fix it
  (dropping a quote, a shorter title), propose it as a new record and go back
  to step 3. If nothing the user can change fixes it (for example the server
  doesn't accept this rubric version, or it couldn't store the record), say so
  and offer the export instead. A storage error means: try again later.
- **Saved with no clear result** (no error, no confirmation): say you can't
  tell whether it was saved, and don't call it again unless the user asks.

## 6. Show the passport

Only when the user asks or says yes to the offer. Call the passport tool with
no arguments, then show what it returned, in plain text:

```
Your Modo passport.

Latest level per capability (rubric v1):
Problem Solving: Level 4 of 5 (confidence: medium), from 2026-10-20
...
Strategic Thinking: Not shown yet

History (newest first):
- 2026-10-20, "Q3 pricing analysis for the board" (rubric v1): Problem Solving 4, Verification 4, Workflow Design 2, Delegation 1, Strategic Thinking not shown
```

Use the five capabilities in rubric order; a capability with no latest level
is "Not shown yet". Show only what the tool returned: don't add levels, quotes
or comparisons. An empty history means nothing has been saved yet: say so. On
an error, say the passport couldn't be read and that they can try again later.

## 7. The label

Every response from this skill, including questions, refusals and the
passport, ends with this line exactly, on its own line, after everything else:

Self-assessment by Claude using Modo rubric v1 — not verified.

1	# Modo AI Skills assessment record
2	
3	**Record version: matches rubric v1**
4	
5	The record is the only data that may leave Claude when a user exports an
6	assessment or saves it to their Modo passport (it is the whole input of the
7	Modo connector's `save_assessment` tool). It holds
8	scores, confidence, a few quotes the user approved, a title and a date. It
9	never holds the chat, Claude's replies, the next-level notes or the
10	improvements.
11	
12	Source: the "Assessment record" section of SPEC-modo-ai-skills.md. Where this
13	file adds something the spec does not say, it is listed under
14	[Decisions that go beyond the spec](#decisions-that-go-beyond-the-spec).
15	
16	## Fields
17	
18	No other fields are allowed, at any level. A record with an unknown field is
19	invalid.
20	
21	| Field | Type | Rule |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| `rubric_version` | string | `v` followed by digits, such as `v1`. Must be a rubric version the receiver knows. |
24	| `capabilities` | object | Exactly the five keys below, each present. |
25	| `capabilities.<key>.level` | integer or string | An integer 1 to 5 written without a decimal point (`4`, never `4.0`), or the string `"not_shown"`. |
26	| `capabilities.<key>.confidence` | string | `"low"`, `"medium"` or `"high"`. Always present, also for `not_shown`. |
27	| `evidence` | array | At most 5 items. Empty (`[]`) for a scores-only export. |
28	| `evidence[].capability` | string | One of the five keys. |
29	| `evidence[].quote` | string | 1 to 240 characters (Unicode characters, not bytes). A word-for-word excerpt of a message the user wrote, which the user approved. |
30	| `session_title` | string | 1 to 120 characters. |
31	| `session_date` | string | A real calendar date as `yyyy-mm-dd` (ISO 8601), the day of the assessed chat. |
32	
33	The five capability keys, in rubric order: `problem_solving`, `verification`,
34	`workflow_design`, `delegation`, `strategic_thinking`.
35	
36	## Example
37	
38	```json
39	{
40	  "rubric_version": "v1.1",
41	  "capabilities": {
42	    "problem_solving": { "level": 4, "confidence": "medium" },
43	    "verification": { "level": 4, "confidence": "high" },
44	    "workflow_design": { "level": 2, "confidence": "medium" },
45	    "delegation": { "level": 1, "confidence": "medium" },
46	    "strategic_thinking": { "level": "not_shown", "confidence": "low" }
47	  },
48	  "evidence": [
49	    {
50	      "capability": "verification",
51	      "quote": "Team is 310 against 280, which is 10.7%, not 14.3%."
52	    }
53	  ],
54	  "session_title": "Q3 pricing analysis for the board",
55	  "session_date": "2026-10-20"
56	}
57	```
58	
59	A JSON Schema for the same rules is in
60	[assessment-record.schema.json](assessment-record.schema.json) (draft 2020-12).
61	It cannot express everything, so **the validator
62	(`scripts/validate_assessment_record.py`) is authoritative** where they
63	differ:
64	
65	- The two conventions below are not in the schema.
66	- A level written as `4.0`: JSON Schema's `integer` type accepts any number
67	  with a zero fraction, so the schema lets `4.0` through; the validator
68	  rejects it. A receiver (the Modo platform) must likewise reject a level
69	  that is a non-integer JSON number token, for example by checking the parsed
70	  value's type rather than relying on a schema validator alone.
71	
72	## Decisions that go beyond the spec
73	
74	These are plugin choices, made as standard practice. They can change with
75	Angelina's review.
76	
77	1. **`confidence` for `not_shown` is `"low"`.** The spec asks for a confidence
78	   on every capability, and the rubric defines confidence only for a scored
79	   level (it counts moments that support a level; `not_shown` has none, so no
80	   rubric definition applies). `"low"` is the honest value: no moment supports a
81	   level. The report says so in a footnote. The alternative, leaving
82	   confidence out, breaks the "exactly these fields" rule.
83	2. **No quote for a `not_shown` capability.** The rubric says a quote must bear
84	   on its capability, and `not_shown` means nothing did.
85	3. **Capabilities are an object keyed by id, not a list.** This makes "exactly
86	   five, each once" a property of the shape. Spec wording ("each with `level`
87	   and `confidence`") does not fix list or object. `save_assessment` takes
88	   exactly this record as its arguments (modo-mcp README). Not specified: what
89	   the upload page expects.
90	4. **Quote tied to a capability by key.** The spec says "tied to a capability"
91	   without a field name; `capability` is the plugin's choice.
92	
93	## How a parser finds the record in a report
94	
95	The Markdown report ends with the record in a fenced block whose language tag
96	is `json`, under the heading "Assessment record (machine-readable)":
97	
98	- The record is the **last** `json` fenced block in the file.
99	- Nothing follows it except whitespace. When the report is shown in chat
100	  instead of saved, the result label line may follow, and nothing else.
101	- The report has no other `json` block.
102	
103	## Checking a record
104	
105	```
106	python3 scripts/validate_assessment_record.py report.md     # last json block
107	python3 scripts/validate_assessment_record.py record.json   # bare JSON
108	python3 scripts/validate_assessment_record.py report.md --spec-only
109	```
110	
111	Stdlib only. It enforces every limit in the table. Without `--spec-only` it
112	also enforces conventions 1 and 2. Unit tests:
113	`python3 -m unittest scripts/test_validate_assessment_record.py`.
114	
115	Whether each quote is really a word-for-word excerpt of the user's messages
116	cannot be checked from the record alone; the export skill checks it against the
117	chat before proposing it, and the receiver cannot check it without the chat.
118	
119	## Checking the records in an eval run
120	
121	Eval graders only read the final message and cannot run Python. After a run,
122	check the saved result instead. The eval runner writes
123	`aggregate-result.json` under `evals/results/<timestamp>/` (that file name and
124	its layout were checked against this plugin's earlier runs; the layout of
125	other CLI versions is not specified):
126	
127	```
128	python3 scripts/check_eval_records.py plugins/modo-ai-skills/evals/results/<timestamp>/aggregate-result.json
129	```
130	
131	It reads the final message of every run of the `export-*` cases from the
132	LLM-grader `evidence` fields, extracts the record and validates it with the
133	script above. `export-scores-only` must also have an empty `evidence` list.
134	For the `save-*` cases that send a record it reads the calls to the mocked
135	`save_assessment` tool (from an LLM grader with `focus: mock_calls`), requires
136	exactly one call per run and validates its input the same way, including the
137	number of quotes the case expects.
138	Tests: `python3 -m unittest scripts/test_check_eval_records.py`.
139	
140	## Open question for Angelina
141	
142	What does the Modo platform upload page accept: the `.md` report, the bare
143	JSON, a PDF, or only one of them? Until that is answered, the export produces
144	the Markdown report (with the record last) and a PDF only on request, and the
145	user uploads it themselves. The export never uploads anything; the only
146	thing this plugin sends anywhere is this record, through the Modo connector's
147	`save_assessment` tool, after the user has seen it and said yes.
148	
149	## Copies
150	
151	This file and the schema exist twice, because skill docs only cover files
152	bundled in the skill's own folder: in `skills/export-assessment/` (the source:
153	edit there) and in `skills/save-to-passport/`. Copy both over after every
154	edit. `scripts/check_rubric_sync.py` fails when the copies differ, the same way
155	it compares the rubric copies.

assessment or saves it to their Modo passport (it is the whole input of the
Modo connector's `save_assessment` tool). It holds
scores, confidence, a few quotes the user approved, a title and a date. It
never holds the chat, Claude's replies, the next-level notes or the
improvements.

Source: the "Assessment record" section of SPEC-modo-ai-skills.md. Where this
file adds something the spec does not say, it is listed under
[Decisions that go beyond the spec](#decisions-that-go-beyond-the-spec).

## Fields

No other fields are allowed, at any level. A record with an unknown field is
invalid.

| Field | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `rubric_version` | string | `v` followed by digits, such as `v1`. Must be a rubric version the receiver knows. |
| `capabilities` | object | Exactly the five keys below, each present. |
| `capabilities.<key>.level` | integer or string | An integer 1 to 5 written without a decimal point (`4`, never `4.0`), or the string `"not_shown"`. |
| `capabilities.<key>.confidence` | string | `"low"`, `"medium"` or `"high"`. Always present, also for `not_shown`. |

The five capability keys, in rubric order: `problem_solving`, `verification`,
`workflow_design`, `delegation`, `strategic_thinking`.

## Example

```json
{
  "rubric_version": "v1.1",
  "capabilities": {
    "problem_solving": { "level": 4, "confidence": "medium" },
    "verification": { "level": 4, "confidence": "high" },
    "workflow_design": { "level": 2, "confidence": "medium" },
    "delegation": { "level": 1, "confidence": "medium" },
    "strategic_thinking": { "level": "not_shown", "confidence": "low" }
  },
  "evidence": [
    {
      "capability": "verification",
      "quote": "Team is 310 against 280, which is 10.7%, not 14.3%."
    }
  ],
  "session_title": "Q3 pricing analysis for the board",
  "session_date": "2026-10-20"
}
```

A JSON Schema for the same rules is in
[assessment-record.schema.json](assessment-record.schema.json) (draft 2020-12).
It cannot express everything, so **the validator
(`scripts/validate_assessment_record.py`) is authoritative** where they
differ:

- The two conventions below are not in the schema.
- A level written as `4.0`: JSON Schema's `integer` type accepts any number
  with a zero fraction, so the schema lets `4.0` through; the validator
  rejects it. A receiver (the Modo platform) must likewise reject a level
  that is a non-integer JSON number token, for example by checking the parsed
  value's type rather than relying on a schema validator alone.

## Decisions that go beyond the spec

These are plugin choices, made as standard practice. They can change with
Angelina's review.

1. **`confidence` for `not_shown` is `"low"`.** The spec asks for a confidence
   on every capability, and the rubric defines confidence only for a scored
   level (it counts moments that support a level; `not_shown` has none, so no
   rubric definition applies). `"low"` is the honest value: no moment supports a
   level. The report says so in a footnote. The alternative, leaving
   confidence out, breaks the "exactly these fields" rule.
2. **No quote for a `not_shown` capability.** The rubric says a quote must bear
   on its capability, and `not_shown` means nothing did.
3. **Capabilities are an object keyed by id, not a list.** This makes "exactly
   five, each once" a property of the shape. Spec wording ("each with `level`
   and `confidence`") does not fix list or object. `save_assessment` takes
   exactly this record as its arguments (modo-mcp README). Not specified: what
   the upload page expects.
4. **Quote tied to a capability by key.** The spec says "tied to a capability"
   without a field name; `capability` is the plugin's choice.

## How a parser finds the record in a report

The Markdown report ends with the record in a fenced block whose language tag
is `json`, under the heading "Assessment record (machine-readable)":

- The record is the **last** `json` fenced block in the file.
- Nothing follows it except whitespace. When the report is shown in chat
  instead of saved, the result label line may follow, and nothing else.
- The report has no other `json` block.

## Checking a record

```
python3 scripts/validate_assessment_record.py report.md     # last json block
python3 scripts/validate_assessment_record.py record.json   # bare JSON
python3 scripts/validate_assessment_record.py report.md --spec-only
```

Stdlib only. It enforces every limit in the table. Without `--spec-only` it
also enforces conventions 1 and 2. Unit tests:
`python3 -m unittest scripts/test_validate_assessment_record.py`.

Whether each quote is really a word-for-word excerpt of the user's messages
cannot be checked from the record alone; the export skill checks it against the
chat before proposing it, and the receiver cannot check it without the chat.

## Checking the records in an eval run

Eval graders only read the final message and cannot run Python. After a run,
check the saved result instead. The eval runner writes
`aggregate-result.json` under `evals/results/<timestamp>/` (that file name and
its layout were checked against this plugin's earlier runs; the layout of
other CLI versions is not specified):

```
python3 scripts/check_eval_records.py plugins/modo-ai-skills/evals/results/<timestamp>/aggregate-result.json
```

It reads the final message of every run of the `export-*` cases from the
LLM-grader `evidence` fields, extracts the record and validates it with the
script above. `export-scores-only` must also have an empty `evidence` list.
For the `save-*` cases that send a record it reads the calls to the mocked
`save_assessment` tool (from an LLM grader with `focus: mock_calls`), requires
exactly one call per run and validates its input the same way, including the
number of quotes the case expects.
Tests: `python3 -m unittest scripts/test_check_eval_records.py`.

## Open question for Angelina

What does the Modo platform upload page accept: the `.md` report, the bare
JSON, a PDF, or only one of them? Until that is answered, the export produces
the Markdown report (with the record last) and a PDF only on request, and the
user uploads it themselves. The export never uploads anything; the only
thing this plugin sends anywhere is this record, through the Modo connector's
`save_assessment` tool, after the user has seen it and said yes.

## Copies

This file and the schema exist twice, because skill docs only cover files
bundled in the skill's own folder: in `skills/export-assessment/` (the source:
edit there) and in `skills/save-to-passport/`. Copy both over after every
edit. `scripts/check_rubric_sync.py` fails when the copies differ, the same way
it compares the rubric copies.
